subject: [PATCH 0/5] KVM: guest_memfd: bind backing memory to a NUMA node

reviews.author: Ackerley Tng
reviews.summary: Reviewer Ackerley Tng suggested alternative approaches to ensure guest_memfd allocations come from a single node, including using cgroups/cpuset, process-level NUMA policy, requesting mmap-ability for memory policy setting, fbind() API, or passing an fd representing a mount with a specified memory policy.
reviews.raw_body:
Instead of a custom API to ensure all guest_memfd allocations come from
a single node, how about these options?

1. Using cgroups/cpuset to constrain allocations (could be troublesome
   if the guest memory is not preallocated, unless the vCPU threads are
   running with the cpuset config)

2. Process-level NUMA policy

3. Why not request the guest_memfd to be mmap-able just to be able to
   set a memory policy?

4. How about something like fbind() that takes an fd and offset range
   instead of mbind(), which has a prerequisite on mmap()?

This doesn't exist yet, but I'm hoping to discuss this at LPC 2026:

5. What if you could pass an fd representing a mount to guest_memfd at
   creation time, so to make all the allocations come from a single node

    Step 1: Create a tmpfs mount, specify mpol for mount to MPOL_BIND
    Step 2: Get some fd representing the tmpfs mount, hand that to
            guest_memfd at creation time
    Step 3: guest_memfd allocations will always come from that tmpfs
            mount, and abide by that tmpfs mount's memory policy.

May I know more about the use case behind this new feature?

reviews.author: Gregory Price (author)
reviews.summary:
Author clarified that the intent of GUEST_MEMFD_FLAG_BIND_NODE is to bind guest memory to a specific target node, not all system memory for a given process, and acknowledged that the desired node may not have eligible memory.

Author acknowledged that requiring a mapping to set node placement defeats the purpose of confidential, host-unmapped guests and plans to enable this for such use cases.

The author is addressing concerns about the scope and implementation of guest_memfd, specifically where the policy lives for random file descriptors (fd's) and how a reclaimed inode's policy is handled. The author acknowledges these limitations but prefers to start with a narrow use-case, considering it less over-engineering than implementing per-file mempolicies.

Author acknowledges that implementing a single-node binding approach is more feasible than using fbind, but expresses uncertainty about the complexity of details.

Author acknowledged that the patch's approach of binding guest memory to a single node is necessary for modeling a confidential VM's topology and explained that this implementation enables the only clear use case.
reviews.raw_body:
for 1 and 2:

the intent is to put the guest memory on the target node, not all system
memory for a given process.  so the scope here is not the same.

in fact at that granularity, the desired node may not even have eligible
memory to host the task's memory.

---

the eventual intent is to enable this for fully confidential,
host-unmapped guest, isolated to a particular memory device.

Requiring a mapping to get node-placement is quite defeating the point.

---

This was a consideration - although it has other limitations and larger
complexities associated with it.

Where does the policy live for random fd's? (inode? address_space?) 

How is a reclaimed inode's policy handled? (lost forever?)

figured i'd start by reducing the scope to the narrowest and clearest
use-case, but I did expect to have the fbind() conversation.

I'm open to it, but it seems like over-engineering.

If you look at tmpfs / shmem, you'll see there is the option for a
default filesystem-wide mempolicy that can be plumbed, but i'm not sure
there's a real usecase for per-file mempolicies that isn't literally
guest_memfd.

---

This i think this is more feasible than something like fbind, but devil
is in the details.

I definitely think it's interesting and would love to chat at LPC!

---

see above - confidential vm whose memory is quarantined to a particular
device, without placing that same burden on the host memory.

~Gregory

reviews.author: Ackerley Tng
reviews.summary:
Reviewer Ackerley Tng noted that a similar problem was encountered where guest memory was charged to the thread's parent memcg instead of the desired memcg, and suggested exploring if this workaround could technically work for NUMA allocations.

Reviewer Ackerley Tng suggested that the policy would be saved at gi->policy, which is where it's currently stored for mbind(), and noted that fd+offset is just another way of referencing offsets to set the policy.

Reviewer Ackerley Tng noted that the patch does not address HugeTLBfs and suggested adding a similar mechanism for configuring HugeTLB page size, but also mentioned that it would not help with memcg since tmpfs does not offer a way to configure them.

Reviewer Ackerley Tng questioned whether lazy allocation is necessary, suggesting that pre-allocating memory using fallocate() before the guest accesses pages might be sufficient.
sentiment_signals: neutral comment without clear concern or suggestion
reviews.raw_body:
We have a similar problem where we wanted only guest memory to be
charged a certain memcg. Currently guest_memfd memory is charge to
mm->owner, which is the thread's parent, so doing the fallocate() in a
thread wasn't good enough. The workaround was to have the fallocate()
done in a separate process (fork) and have the child process's memcg be
set to the desired memcg.

This workaround is kind of awkward, but could it technically work for
NUMA allocations?

---

Off the top of my head the policy would be saved at gi->policy, where
it's stored for mbind() now. fd+offset is just another way of
referencing the offsets to set the policy.

---

Great! :) Cya!

Along the above lines, for HugeTLBfs we'd do something similar, and the
mount's fd would also indicate the HugeTLB page size.

Relating to memcg above, this doesn't really help though, since tmpfs
doesn't offer a way to configure memcgs.

---

Is lazy allocation a requirement for you? (as opposed to fallocate()-ing
before the guest touches pages)

reviews.author: Gregory Price (author)
reviews.summary:
Author acknowledges that the patch does not fully address the issue of ineligible memory, specifically when a node is 100% ZONE_MOVABLE and later unmapped.

Author acknowledges that the patch's approach may not be suitable for all use cases, specifically mentioning anonymous file usage where fbind() means 'put unmapped page cache on node X', but does not commit to revising the patch.

Author acknowledged the reviewer's concern about handling non-mapped guest memory, explained that existing semantics already handle mapped regions, and did not indicate a fix is planned.

Author acknowledged that future support for overcommit is necessary and plans to implement it from the start.
reviews.raw_body:
That is a very clunky work-around, I'm not sure it's good to formalize
that kind of design as an expected user behavior.

Whatever the case, the issue of ineligible memory isn't resolved by
this.  A node may be 100% ZONE_MOVABLE, and later entirely unmapped -
literally no eligible memory for kernel allocations for the task itself.

---

It makes sense for anon use cases like this, but for some random file
where fbind() means "put unmapped page cache on node X" the story is
less clear.

---

The only thing i've considered is something like GPU wanting a file
faulted directly onto its node - but that's a mapped region, and that's
handled by existing semantics.

---

Yes, because eventually some kind of overcommit will be desired. May as
well build it in from the start.

Looking forward to LPC :]

~Gregory

2026-09-09.patch_summary: This patch series adds a new flag to the KVM guest memory file descriptor (memfd) API, allowing users to bind the backing memory of the guest to a specific NUMA node. This is done by creating an MPOL_BIND policy for the requested node and installing it over the whole inode, ensuring that every folio is allocated on the specified node without requiring user-space mbind(). The patch series also includes self-test harness support and testing to validate the new functionality. The approach taken is to simplify the guest NUMA topology by binding a single fd to a host node, rather than interleaving it across multiple nodes, which would defeat placement decisions made by the guest.

reviews.author: Gregory Price
reviews.summary: Raised a concern that creating a VMA for guest_memfd would be hacky and confusing, given its intent to not have a VMA. Asked if there was a series proposing this.

reviews.author: David Hildenbrand (Arm)
reviews.summary: Clarified that the VMA is not necessary for faulting in pages, and suggested using GUEST_MEMFD_FLAG_MMAP to reject faults. Raised questions about the patch's compatibility with shared memory pages.

2026-09-10.patch_summary: The patch aims to bind backing memory for guest_memfd to a NUMA node, but there are concerns about the approach and its compatibility with existing features.
